prompt: Merge sort splits a list in half, sorts each half recursively, then merges them in linear time. Which description of its recursion and running time is right? (n is the number of items.)

options.text: One half-size call and constant extra work: O(log n)
options.explanation: That is binary search, which recurses into only one half and does constant work. Merge sort recurses into both halves and does a linear merge.

options.text: Two half-size calls and a linear merge: O(n log n)
options.explanation: Correct. Two half-size subproblems plus a linear merge: each of the about log₂n levels does about n work in total.

options.text: Two half-size calls and constant extra work: O(n)
options.explanation: This ignores the merge step, which must look at every element. With a constant combine the total would be O(n), but merging costs linear work in every call.

options.text: One call on n − 1 items and linear extra work: O(n²)
options.explanation: This is a split that peels off one element at a time, like quicksort with a worst-case pivot. Merge sort always splits evenly.

workedExample:
Here n is the number of items in the list.

1. **Divide**: split at `mid` into two halves of about n/2 items, and sort each recursively: two half-size calls.
2. **Combine**: merging two sorted lists of total length n is linear work.
3. **Master theorem**: two half-size calls give a critical exponent of 1 (doubling the calls exactly cancels halving the size), and the merge is linear, exponent 1. They match, so every level costs the same.
4. **Recursion-tree check**: level k has 2ᵏ lists of n/2ᵏ items, so n work per level, and halving reaches single items after about log₂n levels. Linear work times logarithmically many levels gives **O(n log n)**.

For a million items that is about 20 levels of a million steps each: a scale estimate, not an exact comparison count.
